newsitem.title: FRANCE: French deficit seen overshooting at moment - paper.
newsitem.headline: French deficit seen overshooting at moment - paper.

text.p: The budget division of the French finance ministry has drawn up a "forecast note" showing that the public deficit, based on current data, could hit 3.8 percent of GDP in 1997, or 3.5 percent including corrective measures, the daily newspaper Le Monde said on Thursday.
The 1998 deficit could reach 4.5 percent, or four percent including corrective measures, the afternoon daily said.
It noted that part of the calculation for this year was an overshoot on the social security deficit, which could come in at 47 billion francs rather than the current estimate of 30 billion.

Earlier, government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said on RTL radio the government saw no budget worries at this stage but would take any steps needed if there proved to be slippage, repeating comments by a finance ministry official on Wednesday.

"We have no budget problems at this stage," Lamassoure said. "Social security spending has also been reined in like never before. This year the pace of economic growth is rising rapidly and revenues will thus start coming back again," he said.
"If we were to note during the year that revenues were not coming in fast enough, then we would have to take additional measures. But we already have a margin of manoeuvre," he said.

Le Monde said the confidential note from the internal budget division of the finance ministry was in the hands of President Jacques Chirac's office and Prime Minister Alain Juppe's office and painted a grimmer picture of the situation than previously.
It said it had asked the finance ministry for the note but had been refused. "Nevertheless, we got confirmation from very good sources, on the preciseness of the figures," it said.

It said the note, a traditional exercise at this time, was to be treated with caution since the ministry division had the task of highlighting "all budget dangers even if there is little chance of them coming true".

It also said there appeared to be "less worrying scenarios" in the note which saw the 1997 deficit at 3.3 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 on the basis of firm economic growth and better revenues.

The government has pledged to bring the public deficit down to three percent of GDP in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998 and to do all that is needed to make the 1997 target required for joining european monetary union at the start of 1999.
Le Monde said the situation for 1998 could prove more tricky than this year as far as government targets were concerned.

It highlighted a well-worn argument that the government had used 37.5 billion francs in France Telecom transfers in its 1997 deficit calculation and would need to find further similar resources in 1998 to ensure a further reduction in the deficit to 2.8 percent of GDP.
The parliament is set to debate 1998 budget needs for the first time in mid-May, which traditionally triggers hefty press speculation about budget woes at this time of year.
Le Monde said France could need to find another 75 billion francs in 1998, the equivalent of one percent of GDP.
Among possibilities that have been raised by some for 1998 included the government taking around 60 billion francs from the Caisses d'Epargne, a savings bank grouping.
